subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The minister has accused us of exaggerating. We do not believe you can exaggerate the dangers that lurk in the extension of these powers for an unlimited time, as is being demanded by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production. We do not believe you can exaggerate when the rights of parliament are being jeopardized. We do not believe you can exaggerate when the sovereignty of parliament is in danger. We do not believe our democracy tolerates a minister of the crown placing himself above parliament and above the rule of law. We do not believe in a dictatorship. If that is exaggeration then perhaps we have exaggerated, but we feel it is better to exaggerate today than to lose our freedom tomorrow.
The other point I wish to make comes from the minister's speech. He said that Canadian industry has not seen the Department of Defence Production in a jam without being willing to contribute toward solving the dilemma. If that is true, and we do not doubt that it is, why in heaven's name is the minister demanding these extraordinary powers over industry on a permanent basis? We are not at war; we are not even in a crisis; we are not in a state of emergency. The minister has complained of the ocean of words which have been spoken in this debate. He can blame only himself and his own stubbornness. All we are saying could be put into two little words; I said six at the beginning, but I now say two: "Protect parliament". All we are asking is the deletion of five little words, "Section 41 shall be repealed."
We on this side listened with great interest this afternoon to the Minister of Finance, and we placed considerable hope in the words he spoke. I should like to conclude with a quotation from Right Hon. Herbert Morrison, another man who knew his parliament. He describes the duties of the opposition as follows:
The duly elected majority must rule; but the opposition has its rights and duties. The opposition. has been elected by its supporters to put their point of view in parliament. And it is in accordance with the spirit of our parliamentary democracy that the government should be prepared to listen to and to consider opposition arguments and representations, for our belief in government by majority certainly does not mean that that majority should act in an arbitrary spirit. It is

Defence Production Act silly as well as intolerable if the government, without considering the merits, assumes that every opposition amendment to a bill or opinion on policy is wrong and, therefore, to be rejected out of hand. Oppositions can be right and governments can be wrong. Therefore, ministers should fairly consider arguments seriously advanced from both sides of the house.
We of the opposition reiterate that statement. Our belief in government by majority does not mean that the majority should act in an arbitrary spirit. Oppositions can be right and governments can be wrong. We ask the minister to give fair consideration to our arguments and to our suggestions when we are in committee.
I must finish with the story of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). This concerns a gentleman by the name of Stephen Decatur. I do not know whether he had any relationship to the minister. In the war of 1812 the British blockade held him powerless for more than two years, during which time he attempted in every possible way to force his way through the ranks of the defenders of Canada's liberty. When he broke out at last and ran for it he was held in battle by the resolute commander of one small British ship until the rest of the blockading squadron could come up. Then, in the words of the United States narrative, he had to surrender.
It could happen to the minister who bears his name as it happened to Stephen Decatur over a hundred years ago. It may happen that the minister will be successful in running the current blockade and may perchance feel he is free, but I warn him-and these are the words of the hon. member for Hamilton West -that he may still encounter storms outside the harbour.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this chamber late this afternoon hon. members witnessed what may well prove to have been a memorable scene in Canadian parliamentary history. It had something of the elements of a climax about it. There has been proceeding in this house for some days now a debate on a government measure the true essence of which, as we have contended before the house, is to confer upon one minister powers which can only be properly described as dictatorial. But the pattern of dictatorship could not be complete as long as it remained open to free members of a free parliament of Canada to voice their opinions. Continual attempts to override parliament, to brush parliament aside and to vest in one minister these sweeping and untrammelled powers were the pattern and design of dictatorship that remained to be completed.


What hon. members saw in this house this afternoon in that climacteric moment was the completion of the design.
The right of hon. members, which we thought was assured to them under the rules of this house, to introduce amendments on second reading is now in process of being taken away from them by government action. The government, which under every concept of responsible government is responsible to this house as the supreme power, has now decided that the right of parliament to talk- that thing for which parliament exists-shall now be taken away from parliament. I may say I shall have some direct words to address to the Prime Minister before I am finished.
May I recall to hon. members that when the vote on the amendment of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) had been completed this afternoon, three members of this house rose to their feet seeking the floor. They rose simultaneously. For the reasons which he explained Mr. Speaker recognized the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), the house leader of the government. He had a motion. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) rose to her feet with an amendment to be introduced on behalf of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, and one of the Social Credit members also was on his feet. Whether he had an amendment to introduce I know not, but at any rate I think it may be assumed that when he was on his feet he had such an amendment.
The motion that was introduced on behalf of the government by the government leader in this house was that the question be now put. That motion, as all hon. members of this house well know, precludes the introduction of any further amendment at this stage of debate, on second reading of this bill. It precludes any further discussion except of the motion itself. Once this motion is carried no further discussion will be possible on second reading of the bill and no amendment of any kind may be introduced by any hon. member-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: On second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
-on second reading. That is what we are talking about. That means that the amendment which the hon. member for Hamilton West sought to introduce cannot be introduced. That means that the amendment which presumably the hon. member of the Social Credit group was about to introduce will not be and cannot be introduced. Other amendments which other hon. members at later stages of the debate on second reading of the bill would have sought to introduce can now never be introduced. Such is the effect, and such is the calculated

effect, of this government motion introduced by the government leader of the house.
Yes, the one thing that remained to parliament, the right to talk, the right to introduce amendments to a government motion for second reading, is now about to be taken from this house. The purpose is plain. The purpose is barefaced. It is to throttle debate in this house on a measure the lasting importance of which before the bar of Canadian history no hon. member of this house dare deny. If hon. members opposite who normally follow the government follow the lead of the government now, this will represent and constitute a ruthless use of power by the majority in the house to suppress discussion in this house of a measure of cardinal importance by hon. members who feel it their duty to discuss it in discharge of their obligations to their constituents and to Canada.
Yes, this motion was introduced on behalf of the government by the government leader of the house. The heir apparent of Liberal leadership in this country has now complied with the invitation that was extended to him and other hon. members of this house just a few days ago by the Minister of Defence Production, when he called upon the house, in asking for these sweeping and dictatorial powers without any limit whatever, and said, "Give me the tools". The Minister of Finance has complied with that request as far as he was concerned by supplying the Minister of Defence Production with one of the tools; that is, the suppression of free discussion in this House of Commons.
Those of us who have retained or sought to retain some respect for Her Majesty's ministers in this country hoped against hope that there might still remain in the minds and hearts of the ministers opposite some allegiance to those liberal principles upon which they have sought in fair weather the endorsation of the Canadian electorate, that there might be, somehow, some lingering loyalty on the part of those ministers to those principles. We knew that the Minister of Defence Production had no place left in his loyalty for liberal principles. The only thing left there is this insatiable demand for power without any limit set by parliament.
There is an old Chinese proverb which is rather plain spoken and, lest I be misunderstood, I shall paraphrase it. It is this: "When the fish rots, it is the head that rots first". There has been evident in this cabinet plain proof of the fact that the dictatorial attitude exhibited this long time by the Minister of Defence Production has now infected the whole cabinet with its contagious blight. The rot has started at the top and is going
Defence Production Act steadily down, permeating all ranks of the cabinet. The government says now it will tolerate no more discussion.

So far as discussion is concerned, the various amendments which under the rules of this house it is possible and proper to introduce on second reading of the bill, especially one of such vast importance as this, are no longer to be permitted to hon. members. If Cromwell were to walk into this house tonight and look at that mace and just repeated those historic words of his, full of contempt for the authority of the elected representatives of the people-"Take away that bauble"-he could not under the rules of this house choose a more effective or direct way of doing it than this government has chosen today.
The government has undertaken now to decide how long parliament shall be permitted to discuss this matter of such great importance. It has taken away the right to introduce amendments. We were made aware on June 28 of the Minister of Defence Production's command, and I am sure hon. members opposite have not forgotten it, when he said the time has come when the government must insist that the bill be passed. This is logical step No. 2, in carrying out that command.
Is this the government's response to the appeal for conciliation made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and echoed in his introductory remarks by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), although the concluding portion of his speech was anything but conciliatory in tone? the official opposition. Yes, perhaps we now have exposed more clearly in its ugly, naked form, the true purpose of this bill. We have said that the undeniable purpose of this bill, indeed the undeniable effect of the bill, would be to deny to parliament the opportunity of keeping any effective control over these vast and sweeping powers vested in the minister and the government by this Defence Production Act.
This manoeuvre now adds this, that it seeks to prevent parliament at this present session from discussing defence production. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think we now have a clearer picture, a clearer view of the true effect of this bill. The bill, as we have said, was to take power from parliament, to deny parliament any participation in and any effective control over the exercise of these sweeping powers in relation to defence production. The effect of the bill was to destroy the power and prestige of parliament.
We have pointed out, sir,-my leader pointed out yesterday, and the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. White) pointed out last night in his excellent speech-how the Defence Production Act takes from individuals in this country one right after another, or could be used for that purpose; the right to counsel when they are under investigation by controllers and officials appointed by the minister; the burden of proof that is cast upon them under the provisions of the bill of disproving charges laid against them under the act; the creation of unnamed offences that we are invited to continue here today, because offences can be created under this act in relation to things that do not exist today, that may arise tomorrow or next year, or in 1958 or 1959. We are being asked to say now that orders made in future are to have the force of law, and the breach of which may be visited with fines of up to $5,000 and imprisonment for up to two years. Here now we have an opportunity of seeing again the deprivation of rights of the Canadian people.

Sir, it is small wonder, I suppose, that certain members in the house do not feel alarmed about this bill. They heard yesterday at long last from the reluctant lips of the Minister of Defence Production the admission that he does not seek to justify this measure on the basis of the existence of any national emergency. Weigh that fact well. He disclaims the existence of any emergency as justifying the continuance of these powers.
Let members keep in mind that the method of placing a time limit upon wide powers has been an effective parliamentary safeguard, honoured by long usage in the history of the mother of parliaments. When the Emergency Powers Act was introduced in 1951 it contained the very effective time limit of a year, and simply had to be continued from year to year if it met the approval of the House of Commons.
As the hon. member for Peace River pointed out in his speech two days ago, the wheat board has a time limit placed upon its powers for the purpose of ensuring strict parliamentary control over those powers. And may I remind hon. members that the greatest landmark in all parliamentary history has been the effective time limit of one year imposed by the British army annual act on the raising of armed forces in that country. This is well recognized parliamentary practice. Ignore it, cast it aside, make no use of it here, and you do so at your peril, at the peril of parliamentary prestige and power, at the peril of our way of life in this country!
The C.C.F. of course have welcomed this measure and given it their strong support. Measures of this kind are inherent in the machinery of socialism. Would that I had time to refer to some of the well recognized socialist texts in this country, books published by the C.C.F., in which they have applauded methods of that kind. But we do not need to refer to those books, because we in this debate have heard the plaudits heaped upon this measure by members of the C.C.F. in this House of Commons.
They want the bill to have second reading before consideration is given to any change or amendment that would safeguard the maintenance of parliamentary control. This measure may be good socialism; but I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I tell this House of Commons, that it is bad democracy.
Yes, this is a bill that creates two kinds of ministers. There is the super minister, the Minister of Defence Production, and then there is the ordinary garden variety of ministers. There are two types, the big type with all the powers, and then the ordinary variety.
Sir, in my closing words may I say this, and I am addressing myself particularly to
Defence Production Act hon. members opposite who normally support the government. I addressed them particularly when I spoke as the first opposition speaker in the debate on June 7. I say to them that the ultimate responsibility for the maintenance of parliamentary safeguards and parliamentary control over these powers and, in the light of what has been attempted today by the government, responsibility for the maintenance of the good name of parliament as a place where free men can freely debate the affairs of the Canadian people, rests upon them, because they are the majority. It should not be left to members of the opposition to defend the rights of parliament, for these are the rights of all Canadians and the rights of all members of parliament.
There is heat and discomfort here. There is interference with summer plans of members. That affects all of us. But this measure has been brought on now, by government design. We received an increase in our parliamentary indemnities last year. I take it that when we received that increase we meant to give service for what we received. But I am not basing my appeal upon dollars and cents. I am appealing to the good conscience of all hon. members in this House of Commons; I am appealing to their duty to maintain parliamentary institutions unsullied and unabridged, in all their strength and vigour.

I do not expect my colleagues opposite to agree with my conclusion, but I have heard many expressions of opinion about this debate, about its effectiveness and about the spirit shown by the opposition in a cause which they consider worth fighting for. May I ask what courses are open to the government on this particular point? The first course, which is suggested by the Winnipeg Free Press as the only honourable course open to the government, is to drop the bill. That is not the only course. The minister has come to the conclusion, as he says on legal advice, with which I cannot agree, that it is impossible to separate this act into two parts, one continuing the Department of Defence Production and the other granting special powers to that department.

Defence Production Act As I have said, it is not an easy thing. The act is a unit and was written as a unit.
As a matter of fact this act is a most remarkable legal document. It is not the outgrowth of any draftsman's consecutive work. It has been built up brick by brick. It is a pyramid which has grown and was constructed from 1940 onward. It carries forward all of the experience of the department of munitions and supply, which had very competent legal advisers. The experience which they obtained in meeting every problem that arose in the enforcement of the defence program in time of war is contained in the act. Therefore they built up an instrument which to my mind has no loophole, no way of escape from the overriding authority of the government if it wishes to exercise that authority.
Therefore this act is a rather remarkable document as it stands. As I say, it is a unit. It is something which has been improved and polished until today, I agree with the minister, it is not an easy task to take the departmental authority for the Department of Defence Production out of the act and consider it as a usual departmental act such as that creating the Department of Public Works or any other department. On the other hand, they should take such powers as the government is prepared to stake its reputation on as being necessary, and put them in a part which would be limited as to time. That is what the two ministers who have spoken have hinted at. That is one course.
I suggest that if the government had been serious they would by this time have had a pattern for the repair of this act. They have known the attitude of the opposition since June 7, and in the interval of 30 days it should have been possible to produce some pattern of repair of this act along the lines which have been hinted at by government members themselves, so we would have before us when we go into committee the assurance of certain modification which had been explained, which was specific and which was understood before we abandoned our position in this debate. If that course had been followed the government necessarily would have had to announce some specific program of amendment. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton, that is precisely what the government failed to do when it made its proposals today.
For example, it might have been stated by the Minister of Defence Production or by the Minister of Finance, when the suggestion was made that the government was prepared to take a certain course in committee, that they would segregate clauses 24, 25, 26, etc., whatever clauses they were prepared to deal with,

Defence Production Act and deal with them in a different way from the act as a whole. If that had been done, then the opposition and other members of the house would have known at this point what course the act would take and would have had some assurance that they could abandon the only weapon they had to meet the government's determination, the weapon of argument on second reading.
It is very clear what the ministers have said and what the government has done. The proposition of the Minister of Defence Production was too conditional; it was full of such conditions as "maybe" and "possibly". No certainty could be placed upon it. The Minister of Finance was no more specific when it came his turn. He suggested that the government might make some change in the bill if it were now permitted to go to the committee. In fact the government has not committed itself to any degree on which any hon. member of this house could rely. All we have is simply an expression of intention to consider. Instead of doing that which I suggest to this house is the second course to the abandonment of the bill, the government has attempted to put a lid on the debate.
There was some appearance of response by the government to the appeal made by the opposition, by the leader of the C.C.F. party and earlier by the leader of the Social Credit party. There was some appearance of response to the appeals to deal properly with this unreasonable act and to find some reasonable basis of compromise. All that we have evoked from the government is a request to trust them to do the right thing in committee, or else closure, the lid, the steamroller will conclude the matter. We do not know at this point what to expect when we get into committee. Perhaps before we get there the government will have pulled itself together and prepared some concrete amendment, some patching-up as I have called it of the act which we can then consider. Certainly if the government wishes to save time that is the best means of doing so.
It may help the government in its consideration of this matter, and I hope it is still considering the matter, to look at the present position of the department. During the course of this debate I have heard no attempt on the part of the government to deal with the activities of the department. There has been an assertion or indication by the minister of four or five lines of major activity, but there has been no review of the activities of the department as such. There has been no indication of the functions and activities at this point of time. There has been general agree-

ment that there should be such a department. This has been repeated to the point where there is no need for me to repeat it. We must bear that in mind in considering what the department does.
The second problem, of what powers it should have, might emerge from a consideration of the activities. I am going to ask the house to consider with me for a few minutes the latest report of the Department of Defence Production, which is for the period from January 1 to December 31, 1954. This is not a very recent report by any business standard, as it is some six months old, but it is perhaps a recent report by the standard of government departments, which usually report somewhat more tardily than would an efficient business organization. In any event, the latest report we have is to December 31, 1954.
Before looking at the activities of the department as described in this report let me take you to the first report of the department in 1951. We will see there what its original purpose was under the stress of the crisis in Korea. The Department of Defence Production was established on April 1, 1951 by the proclamation of the act we are now being asked to extend in order to carry out the procurement functions of Canada's expanded defence program. The new department assumed the responsibilities previously discharged under the direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce by the Canadian Commercial Corporation in so far as defence procurement was concerned, and by the Department of Trade and Commerce relating to essential materials under the Defence Supplies Act.
I digress here to recall that the Defence Supplies Act contains fairly broad provisions for the procurement of defence supplies. It was designed for peacetime operation, but was suspended by reason of the enactment of the Defence Production Act and would come into effect today if the Defence Production Act were repealed.
The responsibilities of the department in 1951 were said to be summarized as, first, the procurement of all requirements of the Department of National Defence and, second, to take steps necessary to ensure an adequate supply of materials to support the defence procurement program. It states in this report of 1951:
The Defence Supplies Act provided the minister with basic powers to carry out the procurement functions with which he was charged, but was not considered adequate to meet the situation which resulted from the decision to embark on a substantially expanded defence program. Accordingly, the Defence Production Act . . . was enacted.

Here is the opinion that was expressed at the time. On page 14 of the 1951 report it is stated:
Although the powers now in effect are virtually the same as those which existed during the last war, it has been understood that these powers would be used to the minimum extent necessary. The comparative simplicity of the Canadian industrial economy and the full co-operation of industry have made unnecessary any elaborate system of controls in order to meet the requirements of defence and defence-supporting industries.
There you have it. In 1951 the Canadian economy was such that any elaborate system of controls was unnecessary. That program which was undertaken in 1951 is described in the report of December 31, 1954, of the Department of Defence Production, and I think it is very significant to note how the work of the department has been put in hand and organized to the point where it is now beginning to taper off. In some respects it is diminishing, and it is organized on a businesslike basis, which gives anything but a picture of emergency activity by a wartime department. This is what is said about the present activity of the department, on page 9 of the report:
The department is charged with the procurement of those goods and services required by the Canadian armed forces under the present defence program. It also acts as buying agent for the Canadian civil defence program and for the Canadian Commercial Corporation, a crown company primarily responsible for the purchase in Canada of goods required by foreign governments, including requirements under the Colombo plan and other international agreements.
The only thing there that might warrant exceptional powers is the continuing defence program, with which the report deals further in these terms:
Continuing shifts in the emphasis on the various aspects of the defence program required a number of changes in the internal organization of the department. The office of the co-ordinator of production, which had been responsible for the over-all direction of the ammunition, electronics, gun, machine tool, mechanical transport and shipbuilding divisions, and Defence Construction (1951) Limited, was abolished during the year.
There is a complete abolition of part of the department.

This is getting now to the point of residual operations.
-formerly handled by branches and divisions now disbanded and to assist in co-ordinating the work of the department as a whole.
Defence Production Act
Then it deals with personnel. The personnel was reduced from 1,631 to 1,509, a reduction of the order of 8 or 9 per cent. It says:
This staff reduction was made possible as a result of the completion of the work of the materials and small industries divisions at the end of 1953, and a lessening in activity by the Pinetree project office, the economics and statistics branch, and certain head office sections of the general purchasing branch.
We hear a good deal about the needs of the early warning line, but there is a lessening in the activity of the Pinetree project office. Then there is another significant factor about the department:
The number of key personnel on loan from industry was sharply reduced during the year.
We all know the activities carried on under the right hon. minister brought great credit to many men in Canadian industry and business who volunteered their services in wartime. Many of them have again volunteered their services or have been loaned by industry to the department.
By the end of 1954 there were 23 men from industry employed under the Defence Production Act, four serving the department without salary. The number of senior personnel serving on the basis of partial salary or honorarium was reduced from 20 to 9 during the year.
There you have a further reduction. Then, Mr. Speaker, the number of crown companies that served this department was reduced:
The number of crown companies associated with the department and reporting to parliament through the Minister of Defence Production was reduced from 8 to 5 during the year. This change was the result of the transfer on April 1, 1954, from the Minister of Defence Production to the chairman of the privy council committee on scientific and industrial research, of responsibility-

for three of those corporations. These are not emergency activities. These are scientific and research projects which have been transferred entirely from the Department of Defence Production. The opening sentence of the main report in 1954 acknowledges this by saying:
At the end of 1954 almost four years of procurement and construction for Canada's expanded defence program had been completed. The initial build-up of the country's defence potential was largely completed during the past year and, in line with the long term needs of the armed forces, the emphasis was shifted to the scheduling of production to meet a continuing high level of defence procurement.
There is a significant comment on page 13:
Defence industries had no difficulty during the year in obtaining their necessary requirements of essential materials and skilled manpower, and no domestic controls were required.

Defence Production Act This is in the report of the minister on the work of his department, and indicates that defence industries had no difficulty during the year in obtaining their necessary requirements of essential materials and skilled manpower, and no domestic controls were required. That is the present state of activity in the procurement of supplies for defence projects. In the words of the department itself, it does not indicate a very great state of urgency requiring controls of an unlimited order such as we have been protesting in the course of this debate.
On motion of Mr. Michener the debate was adjourned.
